title: Transactional trace & latency playbook for batched inference
content:
Purpose:
This is a hands-on playbook for investigating tail latency in our token-serving pipeline where batching, KV-cache behavior, and routing fallbacks interact. It combines clear metric definitions, trace/span conventions, dashboard sketches, and an investigation run sequence that non-expert oncall engineers can follow.

Scope and context:
- Focus: latency sources visible from the API edge through the serving runtime to the GPU worker. Not a deep dive into model quality or embeddings cost.
- When to use: persistent tail latency regressions, repeated SLO breaches, or complex incidents where traces show many short-lived spans across components.
- Assumptions: spans are present for request-accept, queueing, dispatcher, batch-assemble, kv-lookup, token-generation, stream-sink, and fallback model call.

Metric definitions (canonical names and intent):
- api.request_latency_ms: end-to-end latency from ingress accept to last byte sent (p95/p99 primary).
- queue.wait_ms: time request spent in scheduler queue before being dispatched to a worker. (high impact on tail).
- dispatcher.dispatch_time_ms: time taken to assign request to a worker and prepare routing decisions.
- batch.assemble_ms: time to build a batch (includes serialization, prefix concatenation).
- batch.size: integer batch size for each assembly event. Capture distribution (p50/p90/p99) and max.
- kv.cache_hit: boolean per-request marker for prefix/long-context cache hit.
- kv.cache_hit_rate: fraction of requests with kv.cache_hit==true over sliding window.
- kv.lookup_ms: latency for KV lookups when miss or partial hit.
- compute.token_step_ms: per-token compute time on the accelerator (aggregate as per-sequence average).
- model.fallback_rate: fraction of requests routed to fallback model variants or slower tiers.
- worker.eviction_count: number of cached KV/weights evictions per worker per minute.
- infra.cpu_wait_ms: time workers spend waiting on IO (e.g., mmap, pagefaults) — correlated with cold-starts.
- s3/asset_open_ms: time to open model/quant files (for on-demand loads).

Tracing conventions (span names + attributes):
- Span naming: ingress.accept -> queue.wait -> dispatcher.route -> batch.assemble -> kv.lookup -> worker.compute -> worker.stream_sink
- Key span attributes (tags): model.name, model.version, batch.size, tenant.id (if present), kv.hit (true/false), region, hw_type (A100/V100/CPU), fallback_reason, trace_sample_reason (debug/auto).
- Trace linking: attach job_id and batch_id to all spans in a batch; ensure span_id parity so we can group per-transaction and per-batch.
- Sampling: default adaptive sampling: sample 1% of normal traces, 100% of traces where api.request_latency_ms > p99_baseline OR where kv.cache_hit==false AND batch.size>median+2*IQR. Keep a small reservoir of randomly sampled low-latency traces to detect regressions in distribution.
- Annotations: when we detect routing fallbacks, emit an event span fallback.reason with details (out_of_capacity, model_unhealthy, quant_mismatch).

Dashboard sketches and key panels (operator-first):
- Latency heatmap: horizontal axis = request size (tokens), vertical axis = batch size, color = p99 latency. Purpose: find combinatorial corners (large token + small batch -> expensive).
- Stacked latency waterfall per quantile: show contributions of queue.wait / batch.assemble / kv.lookup / compute / stream_sink for p50/p90/p99.
- Batch size distribution by model: fraction of requests per batch size over 5m sliding window. Alert on sudden shift to very small batches.
- KV hit-rate trend: model-scoped and global. Link every drop >5% absolute to worker.eviction_count and s3/asset_open_ms.
- Fallback-rate and top reasons: pie + top-k reasons list linked to capacity and model-health metrics.
- Worker hotlist: workers with highest compute.token_step_ms and highest pagefaults. Useful for detecting noisy neighbors or degraded hardware.
- Eviction / memory-use panel: track per-worker KV memory and eviction spikes.
- Trace-sampled incident view: pinned panel showing 10 representative traces (p99, p95, p50) with span durations in stacked bars.

SLO mapping and alert thresholds (example):
- API SLO: 99% of requests < 350ms (global p99 target).
- On-call alert (Severity P1): p99(api.request_latency_ms) > 2x SLO for > 10m OR error budget burn > 40% in rolling 1h.
- On-call alert (Severity P2): kv.cache_hit_rate drop > 10% relative baseline AND p95(api.request_latency_ms) increased > 20% in 15m.

Investigation runbook (step-by-step):
1) Baseline check: confirm p99 and p95 on the last 60m, compare with previous 24h baseline.
2) Heatmap quick scan: open latency heatmap, look for hot cells (large token x small batch or small token x tiny batch).
3) Trace sampling: fetch 20 p99 traces in affected window. Check which spans dominate time (queue.wait vs compute vs kv.lookup).
4) If queue.wait dominant:
   - Check scheduler queue depth and worker capacity (reserved pools vs autoscale events).
   - Look for routing fallbacks increasing load on slower pools.
   - If autoscaler recently scaled down, check cooldown windows and scaling events (link to release notes).
5) If kv.lookup dominant or kv.cache_hit_rate low:
   - Inspect eviction stats and recent model rollouts (new model may change cache geometry).
   - Verify asset load latencies (s3/asset_open_ms) and transient object store errors.
   - Consider increasing prefix cache TTL or pre-warming critical keys for the hot route.
6) If compute dominant:
   - Inspect model.version and quantization flags on traces. Look for mixed quantization (some workers landing on int8, others float16).
   - Check worker-level metrics (pagefaults, GPU SM utilization, cublas/cuda errors).
   - If hardware degraded, isolate traffic from the problematic worker and trigger remediation.
7) For fallback-related noise:
   - Identify fallback.reason and check upstream serving health. If fallback due to out_of_capacity, prioritize traffic or enable automatic spillover.
8) Mitigations to try (low-risk ordered list):
   - Temporarily divert a small % of traffic to a stable variant (canary rollback).
   - Increase worker pool for the hot model for 5–15 minutes.
   - Adjust batching policy: increase max batch window to capture more batching during spikes (watch latency impact).
   - Pre-warm KV cache for known hot keys.

Notes on instrumentation gaps we've observed:
- Missing per-batch identifiers in some old dispatcher spans — add batch_id for every dispatcher -> worker mapping.
- Worker-side micro-eviction logs are not consistently correlated with spans; add eviction_count attribute to compute spans.
- S3/asset open events are sometimes aggregated; emit per-request asset_open_ms when on-path.

Operational guidance for dashboards and ownership:
- Dashboard ownership: eng-observability to own global heatmap and SLO panels; product-modeling to own model-scoped panels and cache-key semantics.
- Dashboard TTL: default 90-day retention for metrics; keep synthetic p50/p99 traces pinned for 30 days for postmortems.
- Runbook exercise: schedule a quarterly tabletop to walk through a simulated high-tail-latency incident using these steps.

Open questions / follow-ups (next actions):
- Add explicit batch_id propagation in tracer library (owner: serving-runtime, ticket: OBS-7423).
- Prototype adaptive sampling rule that biases towards low-kv-hit high-batch traces for earlier detection (owner: applied-ml).
- Investigate whether sequence-length bucketing in the heatmap should be log-scaled for better visual coverage (owner: observability-ux).

Appendix: quick checklist for oncall (copyable):
- Check p99/p95 vs baseline (60m vs 24h).
- Inspect latency heatmap and batch size shift.
- Pull 20 p99 traces and inspect span waterfall.
- Check kv.cache_hit_rate and worker.eviction_count.
- Look for recent deploys/rollouts and autoscaler events.
- If immediate mitigation required: shift 5–10% traffic to stable variant or scale up worker pool.

End of playbook.
